summary: Specifies the ASN.X representation of encoding instructions for the Generic String Encoding Rules (GSER). ASN.X is an XML representation of ASN.1 specifications. It is an experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a companion note that shows how one set of encoding hints is written in the tidy XML format.

questions: what is asn.x representation of gser instructions
how does asn.x map gser encoding instructions
subtitle: How to write encoding hints for text-based data in a structured XML notation.

tldr.problem: Encoding instructions allow ASN.1 specifications to control how data gets serialized, but they are defined differently for each encoding standard. GSER (Generic String Encoding Rules) needed its own XML representation.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4913 specifies how to express GSER encoding instructions using ASN.X, an XML representation of ASN.1. It defines translation rules for the single GSER instruction (ChoiceOfStrings) and the control section that holds such instructions.
tldr.outcome: Developers can now write GSER encoding instructions directly in ASN.X form, which is valid XML and can be round-tripped with ASN.1 source.

today: RFC 4913 is an Experimental protocol and remains experimental. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
ASN.X is an XML-based way to write ASN.1 specifications. Instead of the traditional text syntax, you write your data structure definitions in XML elements and attributes. This RFC specifies how encoding instructions (optional notes that change how data is serialized) are represented in ASN.X form, specifically for the Generic String Encoding Rules (GSER).

ASN.1 allows type prefixes and encoding control sections to specify how values should be encoded by various encoding rules. However, each set of encoding rules (XER, GSER, RXER, etc.) defines its own notation for these instructions. This document bridges that gap for GSER.
sections.plainLanguage: ASN.X is like rewriting a form from pen-and-paper to a web form. This RFC shows how to move the special instructions from the ASN.1 form to the web form.

sections.title: Encoding Instructions and Translation
sections.content:
An encoding instruction is a directive placed in an ASN.1 specification that changes how abstract values are encoded. GSER is a text-based encoding standard, and its encoding instructions tell the encoder how to handle certain data structures.

The main concept is translation: when you convert an ASN.1 specification to ASN.X (XML form), you must also convert the encoding instructions. The GSER instructions in ASN.1 become corresponding XML elements in ASN.X. The RFC defines the exact mapping: an encoding control section with GSER instructions becomes a <GSER> element item, and within it, specific instruction types (like choiceOfStrings) become child elements with specific attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: When you move from the text form to the XML form, the special instructions move too. A note that says 'write field X first' becomes an XML tag that says the same thing.

sections.title: The ChoiceOfStrings Instruction
sections.content:
GSER currently defines only one encoding instruction: ChoiceOfStrings. This instruction tells the encoder the order in which to try alternatives when encoding a CHOICE type (a data type that holds one of several possible values).

In ASN.X, a ChoiceOfStrings instruction becomes a <choiceOfStrings> element. If the instruction specifies a precedence (an order for trying alternatives), that precedence becomes a precedence attribute. The attribute value is a whitespace-separated list of qualified names corresponding to the choices, telling the encoder which alternative to try first.

Example in ASN.1: [GSER:CHOICE-OF-STRINGS PRECEDENCE utf8 visible] becomes in ASN.X: <GSER><choiceOfStrings precedence='utf8 ascii'/></GSER>.
sections.plainLanguage: ChoiceOfStrings is like saying 'when you have to pick one of several options, prefer this one first.' In XML form, you write that preference as an attribute on a tag.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content:
An ASN.X translation of a GSER encoding instruction is semantically equivalent to the original ASN.1 form. The security properties of the two forms are identical: an application built from ASN.1 with GSER instructions has the same security profile as one built from the ASN.X translation.

RFC 4913 is an Experimental protocol from 2007. It remains experimental and has not been updated or superseded. The translation rules it defines are stable and unchanged.
sections.plainLanguage: Whether you write the instruction in ASN.1 or in ASN.X, the instruction means the same thing and works the same way.
